title: Van Hollen vs. Schumer: The Fight to Lead the New Democratic Majority
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: Democrats just won the Senate. Now one of their own senators wants to replace the man who led them there.
cover_alt: Collage of Chris Van Hollen, Chuck Schumer, the U.S. Capitol and the 2026 Senate map
cover_caption: Collage by Youth Outsider. Photos provided.

figures.alt: Map of 2026 Senate results; striped states flipped to Democrats

body:
Senate Democrats won their majority on Nov. 3. Nine days later, they had a leadership fight. On Thursday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland [announced](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/chris-van-hollen-challenge-chuck-schumer-senate-majority-leader-democrat/) that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, to become majority leader in the new Congress. *"In this election, the American people called for change,"* Van Hollen said in a statement. *"To deliver, we need new leadership."*

Schumer answered within hours. *"I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,"* he said, [pointing to](https://rollcall.com/2026/11/12/van-hollen-announces-bid-for-majority-leader-but-schumer-says-he-has-the-votes/) the caucus's "55 seats and counting," which he called "an amazing result." Democrats flipped at least eight seats in the midterms, and a race in Alaska is still being counted.

Senators who caucus with Democrats, including independents Bernie Sanders and Angus King, will pick their leader by secret ballot in early December. Newsweek [reports](https://www.newsweek.com/chris-van-hollens-chances-of-beating-chuck-schumer-to-become-senate-leader-12709400) the vote is set for Dec. 1. The winner needs a simple majority. It is the first contested race for Senate Democratic leader in decades, [according to PBS](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/van-hollen-to-challenge-schumer-for-senate-democratic-leader).

Van Hollen, 67, was born in Karachi, Pakistan, the son of an American Foreign Service officer, and grew up partly in Pakistan, Turkey, India and Sri Lanka. He served 14 years in the House, chaired the Democrats' House campaign committee from 2007 to 2011, and was elected to the Senate in 2016. He then chaired the party's Senate campaign committee, the job of getting Democrats elected to the Senate.

In recent years he has become a favorite of the party's progressive wing. In April 2025, he flew to El Salvador to meet Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man the Trump administration had wrongly deported there. He has voted repeatedly with Sanders to block or limit weapons sales to Israel.

Only a week before his announcement, Van Hollen told FOX 5 DC he was "not looking to be the next Democratic leader." Then progressive groups such as Indivisible and RootsAction began pushing him to run, and at a post-election gathering of Democrats, he said, *"There should be no coronation of the next Democratic leader."* On Thursday he called the moment a *"generational opportunity"* and said, *"This isn't about any one person, it's about answering that call."*

His case against Schumer is about how Democrats should use their power. He says the party should use the Dec. 11 government funding deadline as leverage to force the Trump administration to end the Iran war. He has promised to restore the Medicaid funding Republicans cut in last year's budget law, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits that help people pay for health insurance, block public subsidies for data centers and push for a livable minimum wage. He has also pledged to stay out of contested Democratic primaries, which Schumer has been criticized for joining, and to keep money from AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, out of the Senate campaign committee. *"We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people,"* he said, [according to ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Politics/schumer-van-hollen-facing-off-senate-majority-leader/story?id=138111386).

Schumer, 75, has his own record to run on. The divisions in the party opened in March 2025, when he sided with Republicans on a spending bill to avoid a government shutdown, angering much of the Democratic base. Later that year, he kept Democrats largely united through a record-long shutdown over health insurance tax credits. He recruited many of the candidates who won this month and helped raise money for them. He has also been working with senators on a 100-day agenda for 2027 that covers health care, tariffs and stopping the Iran war. *"I'm going to win it,"* he told the Associated Press.

Many of his colleagues agree. By Friday, 15 senators and senators-elect besides Schumer had publicly backed him, [according to a tally by The New Republic](https://newrepublic.com/post/217991/full-list-senators-back-chris-van-hollen-leader): Tim Kaine, Angela Alsobrooks, Sheldon Whitehouse, Ruben Gallego, Mark Kelly, Sherrod Brown, Kirsten Gillibrand, John Fetterman, Richard Blumenthal, Brian Schatz, Angus King, Catherine Cortez Masto, Jacky Rosen, Tammy Baldwin and Jack Reed. One name on that list stands out. Alsobrooks is Van Hollen's fellow senator from Maryland, and she is backing the other guy. King, the Maine independent, put the case for Schumer simply: [*"Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?"*](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/van-hollen-to-challenge-schumer-for-senate-democratic-leader) Rosen said Schumer has *"the experience and the fight"* to keep leading.

Van Hollen's confirmed support is smaller but louder. Sanders endorsed him, writing, *"The Democratic Party must CHANGE."* Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon, one of the caucus's senior progressives, [backed him too](https://thehill.com/the-120/6219652-merkley-supports-van-hollen-majority-leader/), as did two progressive senators-elect, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota. *"Democrats need to deliver,"* Flanagan said. *"That starts with new voices in our leadership."* Van Hollen says more than 10 senators have privately pledged to back him, a number that has not been confirmed.

A third group may matter most. Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and senators-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Troy Jackson of Maine, Juliana Stratton of Illinois and Adam Hamilton of Kansas have said they will not back Schumer but have not endorsed Van Hollen. Senators-elect James Talarico of Texas and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire have also withheld their support from Schumer, according to The New Republic. Most of the rest of the caucus, including Sens. Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, has not publicly picked a side.

Van Hollen admits he is behind. *"Am I the underdog? Yes,"* he said, though he called the race "very much in flux." On Sunday, he told ABC's *This Week* that Schumer was trying to "instill fear" in senators who might back him and was spreading "a lot of misinformation," and he said several senators had switched to his side, [the Washington Examiner reported](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/senate/4804139/van-hollen-schumer-misinformation-senate-majority-leader-votes/). He did not name them. Betting markets agree with him: as of Friday, Polymarket gave Schumer an 87% chance of keeping his job, and Kalshi gave him 83%.

Whatever happens on Dec. 1, the race has already exposed a split inside the new majority: whether voters who handed Democrats the Senate were rewarding the party's leaders, or asking for new ones.
credits: Sources: CBS News, Roll Call, The New Republic, The Hill, Washington Examiner, ABC News, PBS NewsHour/Associated Press, Newsweek, Wikipedia. Photos and map provided.
